profile.purpose: A knife-skills tutorial on onions: how cutting direction affects pungency, how to slice them, and the dicing method a mathematician friend's computer model found to give the most even pieces in the fewest strokes. It ends with restaurant-style fine dice and tips for cutting without tears.
profile.thesis: Onion cells are elongated and the onion is radially rather than orthogonally symmetrical, so the direction and angle of your cuts change both pungency and evenness. Slicing pole to pole gives milder onions, and aiming vertical cuts at a point somewhat below the cutting board gives the most even dice.
key_takeaways: Trim the stem end, halve the onion, and peel off the papery skin plus the first tough layer.
Onion cells are longer pole to pole. Pole-to-pole cuts rupture fewer cells and give milder, sweeter onions; orbital cuts, like onion rings, give more pungent ones.
Use a claw grip with the thumb tucked behind. How fast the fingers move back sets slice thickness. When the remaining piece gets unstable, lay it flat.
Batch repetitive prep tasks the way a factory line would.
The traditional grid dice and radial cuts both give uneven pieces. Aiming cuts at a point roughly 0.6 of the onion's height below the board was modelled as the most efficient dice.
Restaurant-style ultra-even dice: separate and stack the layers, then cut them both ways. This is mostly for looks.
Sealing pole-to-pole and orbital slices in separate containers for about 15 minutes demonstrates the difference in smell.

Only a physical barrier fully stops tears (contact lenses, swim goggles). Ski goggles let the gases through, and candles or cold onions help only minimally. A sharp knife helps by slicing cells rather than crushing them.

outline.title: Introduction and preparation
outline.summary: Introduces onion geometry: root and stem ends as poles, orbital versus pole-to-pole cuts. Shows trimming, halving and peeling off the skin plus the first layer, with an anecdote about why.

outline.title: Understanding onion pungency
outline.summary: Explains how elongated onion cells and their sulfur-compound precursors mean cut direction changes how many cells rupture, using a visual aid. Pole-to-pole cuts give milder onions, orbital cuts more pungent ones.

outline.title: How to slice an onion
outline.summary: Demonstrates slicing pole to pole with a claw grip, controlling thickness, and flattening the last unstable piece. Ends with a start-to-finish run on one half.

outline.title: How to dice an onion
outline.summary: Covers batching prep tasks, then compares three dicing methods: the traditional grid, radial cuts, and the mathematically modelled method of aiming below the cutting board. Includes optional horizontal cuts and how to handle the final nub.

outline.title: Fine dicing for salads
outline.summary: Shows a restaurant technique for very even raw onion dice: separating and stacking the layers, then cutting them both ways.

outline.title: Smell test and tips for cutting without tears
outline.summary: Describes a sealed-container test comparing the smell of pole-to-pole and orbital slices. Then reviews anti-tear methods: contact lenses, swim goggles versus ski goggles, candles, cold onions and sharp knives.
